Johnson Circles

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Three equal circles all pass through the same dot; look at the circle through their other three crossings.
How to play: Drag the three coloured centres around the dotted ring, or focus a centre and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, lines and larger triangles.
Show
Look for the math

Three circles with the same radius can all pass through one point. The surprise is that the circle through their three other crossings is exactly the same size. Drag the centres: nothing here is a race or a score, just a picture that keeps its promise.

Where the other crossings are

Let the shared point be O and write the three centres as vectors a, b, c from O. The applet keeps each centre on a circle of radius r about O, so |a| = |b| = |c| = r and each of the three circles has radius r. The circles centred at b and c meet at O and at b + c: from that point to b is |c| = r, and to c is |b| = r. So A = b + c, and likewise B = c + a, C = a + b. These are ordinary vector sums, not a special case.

The fourth circle and the orthocentric system

From Q = a + b + c the distance to A is |b + c - (a + b + c)| = |a| = r, and the same holds for B and C. That is the main theorem: the circumcircle of ABC has the same radius as the original three. Also OA is perpendicular to BC, because (b + c) · (b - c) = |b|² - |c|² = 0; so O is the orthocenter of ABC and the four points form an orthocentric system. Each original centre is the circumcenter of the triangle made from O and the other two of A, B, C, which is why all four small circumcircles have radius r as well.

Rhombi and two homotheties

The points A, Ob, O, Oc form a rhombus: its sides are the equal vectors c and b. The other two rhombi work the same way, which makes AB parallel and equal to OaOb (and independent of where Oc sits). Since Q - a = b + c = A, a homothety with factor -1 about the midpoint N of OQ maps OaObOc onto ABC; N is also the nine-point center of OaObOc. The anticomplementary triangle has vertices A' = 2a, B' = 2b, C' = 2c: a factor-2 homothety about O. Its circumcircle has radius 2r and touches each original circle at the primed point.

What was checked, and one change

The logic test checks the theorem and every property above on a 12×12×12 grid, the opening layout and 400 random centres (2129 layouts in all), comparing every non-degenerate one with a second transcription of the applet's own GeoSDoub.Intersect, GetCircle, Prorate and Barycenter methods. The article's largest-perimeter claim also holds: a line through C meets the two circles again at points whose separation is 2|(b - a) · u| ≤ 2|b - a|, so no triangle with sides through A, B, C can beat A'B'C', and equality happens when each side is parallel to a line of centres. The published page still states the theorem, but its live version now embeds a GeoGebra figure, not the Java applet; a 2010 archive shows the original APPLET CODE="JohnsonCircles". The applet's own "about" box says "Shapes of Constant Width", a leftover from another applet with no effect on the drawing; only its real behaviour is ported here.

Tick "anticomplementary" and then drag one centre: the dashed outer circle always has twice the radius, and the three sides of the large triangle stay parallel to the lines between the centres.
